I’ve been farming these fields in Quzhou for more than forty years. The land here on the North China Plain is flat and fertile, but the growing season is tight, so the only sensible way to make a living is the double-cropping system everyone around me uses: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same plot. I have six mu of good irrigated land. I finished primary school decades ago, but I know this soil and this climate better than any book.

This year I will stick to what works. In early October I will sow improved wheat varieties—something like the Jimai or Shannong lines I buy from the township seed supply store. They stand up well to lodging and give a stable yield. I will prepare the ground with rotary tillage, spread a base dressing of compound fertilizer, and top-dress with urea at green-up and jointing. I will irrigate four times: the winter irrigation to protect against frost, then at jointing, flowering, and grain filling. For pests and weeds I will spray three times—herbicide early, then insecticide and fungicide when the extension station tells me the pests are moving in. I expect about 550 kg per mu if the weather cooperates.

As soon as the wheat comes off the combine in early June, I will plant hybrid maize—Zhengdan 958 or Nongda 372—directly into the wheat stubble without ploughing. There is no time to waste in summer; no-tillage saves labor and keeps moisture in the ground. I will band compound fertilizer at sowing and side-dress urea at the big-trumpet stage. Two irrigations will be enough if the rains hold, one at jointing and one at filling. I will spray for weeds once and for borers and aphids twice. With decent weather that maize should give me 650 kg per mu.

I thought about growing vegetables on a corner plot, but at my age I prefer to keep things simple and focus on the two crops I can manage with my own hands and a little hired help at harvest.
